Extracting Cow Stories

Source: vignettes/cow_stories.Rmd
cow_stories.Rmd

Discover Cow Stories 🐄📖

“Well hello again, my wonderful friends!” I’m Ollie the Otter and I’m back with more data adventures! Remember how we cleaned all that messy cow data in our last vignette? Now we’re going to do something amazing—we’re going to read the personal stories hidden in each cow’s behavior!

Every cow has her own personality, preferences, and social relationships. Some are explorers who visit many different feeding stations. Others are creatures of habit who stick to their favorite spots. Some are bold and frequently displace other cows from feeders, while others are more submissive.

Today, we’ll analyze two fascinating aspects of cow behavior:

  1. Exploratory behavior - Which cows explore many different feeding and drinking stations?
  2. Social dynamics - Which cows frequently replace others at feeding stations, and which ones get replaced?

Grab your data binoculars and let’s dive in!

1. Prerequisites: Clean Data First! 🧹

Before we can analyze cow behaviors, we need clean data. If you haven’t already processed your raw feeder and drinker data, please follow the instructions in the “Data Cleaning” vignette first!

library(moo4feed)   # 🐮 Your cow data helper!
library(dplyr)      # For data manipulation
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'dplyr'
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:stats':
#> 
#>     filter, lag
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:base':
#> 
#>     intersect, setdiff, setequal, union

For this vignette, we’ll use the cleaned data from the previous vignette:

# Load the example cleaned data from the package
data(clean_feed)
data(clean_water)

# If you're using your own data from the cleaning vignette, use this instead:
# clean_feed <- qc_results$feed     # From your QC results
# clean_water <- qc_results$water   # From your QC results

2. Exploratory Behavior: Which Cows Visit Many Bins? 🔍

Cows differ in how widely they explore their environment. Some visit many different feeding and drinking stations, while others prefer to stick to just a few favorite spots.

The unique_bin_visits() function helps us quantify this exploratory behavior:

# Calculate unique bin visits for each cow across all days
bin_visits <- unique_bin_visits(
  feed = clean_feed,            # Our cleaned feed data
  water = clean_water,          # Our cleaned water data
  return_list = FALSE           # Return a single dataframe instead of a list by day
)

# Look at the results
head(bin_visits)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 5
#>   date      cow unique_feed_bins_vis…¹ unique_water_bins_vi…² total_bins_visited
#>   <chr>   <int>                  <int>                  <int>              <int>
#> 1 2020-1…  2074                     20                      4                 24
#> 2 2020-1…  3150                     22                      4                 26
#> 3 2020-1…  4001                     19                      3                 22
#> 4 2020-1…  4044                     25                      4                 29
#> 5 2020-1…  4070                     24                      4                 28
#> 6 2020-1…  4072                     24                      3                 27
#> # ℹ abbreviated names: ¹​unique_feed_bins_visited, ²​unique_water_bins_visited

What’s in this data? 🦦

For each cow on each day, we now know:

  • How many different feed bins they visited
  • How many different water bins they visited
  • The total number of unique bins visited (feed + water)

This tells us which cows are “explorers” (visiting many bins) versus “creatures of habit” (sticking to fewer bins).

Identify your most exploratory cows

Let’s find the cows that consistently explore the most bins:

# Calculate the average number of unique bins visited per cow
avg_bin_visits <- bin_visits |>
  dplyr::group_by(cow) |>
  dplyr::summarize(
    avg_feed_bins = mean(unique_feed_bins_visited),
    avg_water_bins = mean(unique_water_bins_visited),
    avg_total_bins = mean(total_bins_visited),
    days_observed = dplyr::n()
  ) |>
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(avg_total_bins))

# Display the top 10 most exploratory cows
head(avg_bin_visits, 10)
#> # A tibble: 10 × 5
#>      cow avg_feed_bins avg_water_bins avg_total_bins days_observed
#>    <int>         <dbl>          <dbl>          <dbl>         <int>
#>  1  6030          27.7           4.33           32               3
#>  2  6020          27.7           4              31.7             3
#>  3  7018          26.3           4.67           31               3
#>  4  5041          26.3           4              30.3             3
#>  5  7027          27             3.33           30.3             3
#>  6  5067          26             3.67           29.7             3
#>  7  7022          24.7           5              29.7             3
#>  8  7033          25             4.67           29.7             3
#>  9  5137          25.7           3.67           29.3             3
#> 10  5145          25             4.33           29.3             3

3. Social Dynamics: Detecting Replacement Events 🏆

Dairy cows establish complex social hierarchies. One key social behaviour is when one cow replaces another at feeding or drinking stations.

Detect replacement events

Now, let’s use the record_replacement_days() function to detect replacement events across all days in our dataset:

  • The replacement_threshold parameter is critical - if a cow is feeding at a bin, and the next cow that enters the same bin within 26 seconds, it is considered a replacement event. This threshold is validated by preivous studies.
# Process feed replacement events for all days
replacements <- record_replacement_days(
  comb = clean_feed,           # Our cleaned feed data
  cfg = qc_config(replacement_threshold = 26)      # Time gap (seconds) to classify replacement behavior
)

# Look at the first few replacement events for the first day
head(replacements[[1]])
#> # A tibble: 6 × 6
#>   reactor_cow   bin time                date       actor_cow bout_interval
#>         <int> <dbl> <dttm>              <date>         <int> <Duration>   
#> 1        5124     1 2020-10-31 06:07:52 2020-10-31      6020 10s          
#> 2        6020     1 2020-10-31 06:09:44 2020-10-31      6069 11s          
#> 3        6069     1 2020-10-31 06:12:05 2020-10-31      5124 10s          
#> 4        5124     1 2020-10-31 06:13:37 2020-10-31      5067 10s          
#> 5        7010     1 2020-10-31 06:20:15 2020-10-31      7018 11s          
#> 6        7018     1 2020-10-31 06:20:58 2020-10-31      7010 9s

What’s in this data? 🦦

This is a list of data frames, one per day. Each row represents a replacement event:

  • reactor_cow: The cow that was replaced (had to leave the bin)
  • actor_cow: The cow that initiated the replacement (took over the bin)
  • bin: Which feed bin this happened at
  • time: When the replacement occurred
  • date: Which day this happened
  • bout_interval: The time gap between when one cow left and the next arrived

What does this tell us? 🦦

Patterns in replacement events can reveal:

  • Days with high social tension in the herd
  • Changes in social dynamics over time
  • Effects of management changes on social behavior
  • Potential welfare issues when replacement events spike

Importantly, the function validates each replacement event by checking if the actor cow has an “alibi” - if the cow was recorded at another bin when the previous cow left, the event is excluded. This ensures we’re capturing true social replacement events rather than coincidental timings.

4. What’s Next? 🌟

Congratulations! You’ve now started uncovering the hidden stories in your cow data by:

  1. Quantifying exploratory behavior to identify which cows visit many different bins
  2. Detecting replacement events to understand social dynamics in the herd

This is just the beginning of what you can learn from your feeding and drinking data. With these fundamental metrics, you can:

  • Identify potentially vulnerable animals
  • Understand individual cow preferences and habits
  • Track changes in social behavior over time

Ollie’s Final Tips: 🦦

  • The replacement_threshold parameter in qc_config() controls how quickly one cow must replace another to count as a social displacement (default is 26 seconds)
  • Use unique_bin_visits() with return_list = TRUE if you want to analyze bin visits day by day
  • Replacement events can be further analyzed to calculate dominance hierarchies
  • Remember that behavior patterns can change after major events like regrouping, facility changes, or diet adjustments

Keep analyzing, and your cows will keep telling you their stories! 🐄📊
